verdict: ENRICH places/vancouver.md (short paragraph, ~90-120 words, no new page). INSERTION POINT: add a new H2 '## The 2026 Civic Election' immediately AFTER the last sentence of section '## Modern Value Capture: Density Bonusing, Amenity Contributions and the 2026 Amenity Cost Charge', i.e. after the sentence 'The charge is too new for its effect on either housing supply or amenity funding to be assessed.' and BEFORE '## See Also'. SECOND, OPTIONAL one-sentence ENRICH: research/vancouver-empty-homes-tax.md, section '## Design & Rates', after the sentence ending 'and 5% was never levied.[1][2][3]': add that COPE's 2026 platform proposes to reverse the 2023 decision, enforce the tax and phase rates up to 9%. REASON it is not a REJECT: COPE did very well in the Vancouver civic election of 17 Oct 2026 (all 4 of its council candidates, all 4 of its park board candidates and 4 school trustees elected on preliminary results, with its incumbent Sean Orr the top council vote-getter), so the platform is the stated programme of one of the two largest parties on the new council (4 of 10 seats, level with the Greens), not a fringe manifesto. BUT KEEP IT SMALL AND HONEST: the land-value plank is one bullet with no rate, base, mechanism or legal basis; COPE holds 4 of 10 council seats (tied with the Greens), the mayor is Green Pete Fry, whose platform on this was not read; and nothing has been enacted. State it as 'COPE's platform proposes', not as city policy. READING OF THE PLANK (answers the sharer's question): the platform text does NOT say 'land value tax' as a named tax and gives no rate; it says 'Support taxation on land value, capture the land-owner windfalls caused by proximity to public amenities, speculation, and zoning to use for public benefit'. The object is the windfall (unearned value increment) from three named sources: public amenities, speculation, and zoning. Source (3) zoning, i.e. upzoning uplift, and source (1) amenity proximity are land-value-capture / betterment language; 'taxation on land value' in the same clause is compatible with a recurring land tax but is not specified. The sharer's reading (land value capture on upzoning) is supported as the dominant sense; the text neither confirms nor excludes a recurring LVT, and the wiki should say exactly that (the platform 'does not specify the instrument'). Separately, p.25 states a different property-tax plank: 'progressive taxation of property values' / a Mansion Tax, which is a tax on total property (land plus buildings) value, not on land value: do not conflate them.
claim_grade: Platform as to what COPE PROPOSES: A-claim (factual: what a document says), primary document. EDITORIAL 4c tier: COPE is a political party, so Tier 3 for policy (own statements only) and at most Tier 2 as origin/proponent; the platform may NOT be cited as evidence that land value capture works or is desirable. Election outcome: A-claim, but PRELIMINARY: Canadian Press says 'Preliminary results show...'; the City's own page says official results are declared 21 Oct 2026 by 4pm. Sources CP, Tyee, CBC = serious journalism (level 5 of the EDITORIAL 3 source hierarchy); the City of Vancouver declaration will be the Tier 1 source once published, so T1 should re-check after 21 Oct before the sentence is written. verdict: NEW research/bhutta-keys-raajkumar-mortgage-pricing-power.md (suggested slug; category research, tier Supplementary, authors [Neil Bhutta, Benjamin J. Keys, Adithya Raajkumar], year 2026, source_url https://www.nber.org/papers/w35907). Substantive, quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences with placebo, triple-difference and RD checks), national data, three Tier-1-by-rubric authors: it clears the bar for a research page, and the wiki has no mortgage-pricing or intermediary-pass-through page at all (greps below). BE HONEST ABOUT THE LAND LINK: this is NOT a land-rent paper. Its 'rent' is the imperfect-competition / search-friction profit of mortgage lenders and loan officers (Section 2.3 model: all lenders 'earn rents' because some borrowers do not shop), the paper assumes ELASTIC mortgage supply, and the word 'land' never appears in the body. The Georgist-adjacent value is narrow: (a) it is a clean worked case of who captures a demand-side subsidy ('Subsidies delivered through intermediaries may fail to reach intended beneficiaries'), which the wiki treats for land via tax capitalization / subsidy capitalization, and the contrast is instructive: here the capture is by intermediaries under elastic supply and frictions, whereas with land it is by owners under inelastic supply; (b) it is a rent-gradient-frontier datum for finance (EDITORIAL 0: 'finance and credit' is in scope but contested) and an empirical rent-extraction example in a regulated market. Do NOT present it as evidence for LVT or as evidence that mortgage subsidies are capitalised into land prices (the paper does not measure house or land prices). RECOMMENDED PAGE SHAPE: Summary; the programme; design and data; findings (pass-through 31.5-39.3% across specifications; heterogeneity); what it does and does not show; 'Relation to the Georgist case' as a short, hedged section built on the rent-gradient rule; See Also; Sources with the working-paper status noted impersonally. SUPPORTS_OUTCOMES: none strongly. problems/corporate-profits-increasingly-rents is the nearest claim page but concerns corporate markups at the firm level; I would NOT wire it as 'supported_by' (T1 call). Candidate objection lane: none obviously. INBOUND LINKS (>=2 needed): (1) research/cea-2016-market-power.md, See Also (consumer-finance market power at the point of sale, micro-evidence behind the CEA's macro market-power brief); (2) concepts/economic-rent.md, section '## The Neoclassical Redefinition of Rent' (add a one-line example of search-friction rent) or See Also; (3) concepts/rentier.md, section '## The Contested Boundary of "Rent"', as a worked example of an intermediary rent; (4) concepts/financialization-of-land.md, See Also (mortgage-market pricing, with the explicit note that the paper concerns credit pricing not land); (5) concepts/tax-capitalization.md or concepts/common-agricultural-policy.md, See Also, as the contrast case for who captures a subsidy; (6) narratives/the-rentier-economy.md, under '## Research That Supports It', labelled as a frontier/IO example. Wire at least (1), (2) and (4).
claim_grade: B-claim (empirical, quasi-experimental estimate). NBER working paper: by its own cover statement 'They have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to the review by the NBER Board of Directors', so the page must say it is a non-peer-reviewed working paper and the headline numbers are the authors' estimates. EDITORIAL 4c: authors are Tier 1 by rubric (Philadelphia Fed economist; Wharton professor with a peer-reviewed housing-finance record; neither name is in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, so judged by rubric: established academics/central-bank economists with a body of peer-reviewed work on the topic). Evidence-ordering: class 4 (working papers). The paper is framed by its authors as market power in consumer credit, not as land rent: do not up-grade the claim by implication.

'>60% of $1.5 billion' is stated in the abstract, introduction and conclusion but I found NO derivation of the $1.5bn total in the text (grep for 'billion' returns only the four statements and the CBO figures). It is consistent with 100% minus 39.3% baseline pass-through, but that arithmetic is mine, not the authors', and the origin of $1.5bn (which loans, which years, which volume) is not shown in what I read. Do not present '$0.9 billion' as a paper figure.

Wording drift inside the paper: abstract says 'mortgage intermediaries'; body says 'lenders captured'. The unit of the estimate is lender-level pass-through (with loan-officer and lender fixed effects); 'intermediaries' in the sense of brokers or realtors are not separately measured. The authors attribute weak pass-through to non-shopping borrowers and to referrals, and say a decomposition of mechanisms would need data on borrower beliefs and search ('Decomposing the mechanisms ... would require additional data').

Pass-through estimates depend on the rate-point tradeoff (36 bp per point); with a rule-of-thumb 25 bp it is about 50% (fn 25, p.18), and ignoring points it falls to 28% (Appendix E). The 'less than 40%' and '>60%' headline therefore carries a measurable assumption; the page should state the range.

Counter-reading: the authors say dispersion could reflect unobserved lender costs ('high-touch' lenders), and test it by the expensiveness-pass-through correlation. Earlier full-pass-through results for other g-fee changes (Adelino-Ahsin 2023; Kalda et al. 2023 and others) are cited as contrast; the authors speculate the difference is the less-experienced target population. This is a single study of one programme.

Not about land. If a writer wants the 'subsidy capture' parallel, it must be explicitly labelled analogy: the paper assumes elastic supply and finds intermediary capture; land capitalisation arises from inelastic supply. The paper does not show the waiver raised house prices. EDITORIAL 0 rent gradient applies: this sits at the finance frontier.

The FHFA is called 'Federal Housing Finance Administration' once in the intro (sic; the body uses 'Agency'); the sample period inconsistency noted above (2022-2023 in 3.1 vs 2022-2024 in 4.2). Quote carefully.

verdict: REJECT. Reason: the paper is a stylised airport profit-maximisation model (three-stage game: airport sets the per-passenger charge, representative airline sets fare, passengers demand) about whether growing non-aeronautical (retail, parking) revenue disciplines an airport's charges and so weakens the case for ex ante tariff regulation. It does not engage land rent, airport land value, location rent, Ricardian/ground rent, land-value capture, or any rent-capture instrument. 'Rent' in the paper means monopoly-price extraction ('rent logic' of pricing, 'rent-oriented' business model vs. 'platform' logic), a use already covered at the wiki's level by concepts/economic-rent (Smith: rent as a monopoly price) and concepts/government-granted-privileges. 'Land' (земл*) occurs ZERO times; 'location' only as 'the airport's location influences history of cross-subsidy' (one passing mention, journal p.30); the only land-adjacent sentence is a natural-monopoly entry-barrier remark that sites near cities are scarce (journal p.27). Also: niche Russian-language journal, theory plus a counterfactual calibration on accounting data of 5 Russian airports, a policy conclusion (divergence between private and social optimum is not by itself sufficient justification for ex ante regulation) that is neutral-to-deregulatory and has no bearing on Georgist claims. The wiki's natural-monopoly / infrastructure-pricing coverage is indeed thin, but this single paper would not be the right anchor for filling it (canonical sources there are Baumol-Panzar-Willig, Faulhaber 1975 which this paper cites, Laffont-Tirole, Starkie 2002 etc., none verified here). If a later wave builds an infrastructure-pricing concept, the one hook worth recording is that the paper cites Faulhaber (1975, AER) on cross-subsidy and the 'platform' logic of airports; it is not worth a page now. DEFER-not-REJECT only if T1 specifically wants an 'infrastructure monopoly pricing' page; otherwise REJECT.
claim_grade: C-claim (theoretical, stylised model) with a D-style illustrative calibration on 5 airports. EDITORIAL 4c tier: Tier 2/3 by rubric: authors are university economists (a PhD candidate, Zubenko, and a research fellow, Kurdin, per the author notes, p.43) in a niche Russian competition-policy journal (VAK category 5.2.1 per the first page), not a standing body or recognised authority on rent; peer review is asserted by the journal's policy pages but I did not verify review of this specific article. It could never be cited as support for a rent claim on this wiki.
